newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Chinese dissidents fear 26 will be stranded in HK.
newsitem.headline: Chinese dissidents fear 26 will be stranded in HK.

text.p: Dissidents who fled China for Hong Kong said on Thursday time is running out for at least 26 compatriots who could be stranded after Chinese rule in just 19 days' time.
They want sanctuary in the West but face bureaucratic obstacles leaving Hong Kong and fear rough treatment and arrest if they stay.
Scores have already left the territory in the run-up to the June 30 handover by Britain, said dissident Zhang Taisong who last week threatened to set himself on fire in desperation.
Zhang, who was persuaded to abandon self-immolation, said he and at least 25 others were still anxiously awaiting exit permission from the Hong Kong government.
But the one internationally-known dissident here, Han Dongfang, said he was planning to stay on, refusing to prejudge whether his freedom will be curbed.
Han, a leader of the crushed 1989 democracy movement in Beijing's Tiananmen square, predicts there will be no similar crackdowns in China or Chinese-ruled Hong Kong.
Beijing has pledged a hands-off attitude to Hong Kong's free-market way of life for 50 years, but some among the 6.4 million population fear gradual repressive rule.
"I want to leave Hong Kong before the handover," Zhang told Reuters. "Otherwise, the Chinese government will arrange to treat me badly."
Zhang said he helped other dissidents leave China after the June 1989 crackdown in the Chinese capital, then fled to the territory himself in 1993.

"It's not that other countries don't want to accept us, but the truth is that our files are in the hands of the Hong Kong government. Without their assistance, it's impossible for us to leave," he said.
Most of the dissidents fled China illegally and arrived in Hong Kong illegally and are not eligible for automatic residency in the territory.
A government spokesman refused comment on the dissidents' plight.
Zhang said if he failed to leave Hong Kong before the handover, he would try to protect fellow dissidents still here.
Democratic Party legislator Cheung Man-kwong has warned that dissidents could be in danger if they were forced to return to the mainland after the British colony returns to Chinese rule.
But some of those who sought exile in Hong Kong, such as Lu Siqing and Han Dongfang, have decided to stay on after the handover, despite any potential trouble.
"We can't forget the June 4 crackdown and want to help the imprisoned dissidents in China with our best efforts," said Lu.

Up to 55,000 people poured into Hong Kong's Victoria Park last week for a candlelit vigil to mourn the deaths of hundreds, possibly thousands, eight years ago and to demand a release of political prisoners in China.
Authorities talked Zhang out of a threat to set himself on fire at the rally in a bid to force the Hong Kong government to quicken the exit of remaining dissidents.
Lu said he had been warned of repercussions if he stayed on after the handover.
"The Public Security Bureau (police) in China warned my parents that if I stay in Hong Kong after the handover, I will be in deep trouble," he said.
Those dissidents who fled to other countries would gradually give up their fight for democracy, Lu said.
Han, a former labour organiser who spent two years in jail for "counter-revolutionary acts" after Tiananmen, said he could not be sure what to expect until after China took over.
"My freedom may be restricted after the handover, but I can't say that I will have restrictions before I experience them," he said. "I think I can bear what may happen to me, so I choose to stay."
